newsitem.title: UK: Channel tunnel passengers unworried by fire.
newsitem.headline: Channel tunnel passengers unworried by fire.

text.p: Rail passengers at London's Waterloo station said on Tuesday they were unconcerned by a fire in the Channel Tunnel and were ready to travel through it as soon as it reopened.
A fire on a freight train inside the tunnel late on Monday forced the evacuation of 34 people and put eight of them in hospital suffering from smoke inhalation.

No trains were running from London's futuristic Eurostar Channel Tunnel train terminal on Tuesday morning and a planned cake-cutting ceremony marking two years of the service was cancelled after the blaze.
Passengers were being taken by bus to airports to fly to Paris and Brussels.

"I take it all in my stride, I am not concerned," said retired insurance worker Paul Wormleighton. "We went through the tunnel in May and it was marvellous. You get accidents in any part of the world."
Taxi driver Doug Sadler was disappointed not to be allowed to travel through the tunnel, as the trip under the English Channel was his main reason for going to Paris.
"I wanted to go on the Eurostar, that's why I'm going to Paris," he said. "I think I prefer the tunnel to the aeroplane because I don't like flying."
His wife Maureen agreed: "It's just one of those things that happen. It's my birthday -- what a birthday."
Frenchwoman Ruth Sands was equally phlegmatic: "I've travelled enough in my life not to worry about anything."
Rail worker John Laver, on a trip to Brussels, said he would have "no hesitation" in taking the tunnel again once it reopened.

"You just build up your own paranoia if you are not careful," he said. "People travel on the underground in London every day, but I suppose the distance between stations is a bit further with the Channel Tunnel."
The tunnel fire happened on the ninth anniversary of a fire at London's Kings Cross underground station in which 30 people died.
Dutch student Yvonne Kok, from Zwolle in The Netherlands, agreed there was little to worry about in the tunnel.

"I am not worried about going through the tunnel again. I think they have very good security and they know what to do," she said. "They have been arranging things and trying to get everyone back home."

The only dissenting voice in a straw poll of passengers at the Waterloo terminal came from Lisa Quinn, taking her children Taylor, aged five months, and four-year-old Libby to the Eurodisney theme park, near Paris.
"I'm not too keen on this at all," she said. "I was dubious as to whether I should come here. I'd much rather fly."

The tunnel blaze came at a bad time for British Deputy Prime Minister Michael Heseltine, who was at Waterloo to launch a document called A Competitive Capital -- The Government Strategy For Enhancing London's Competitiveness.

He was expected to laud the contribution the Chunnel trains had made to the capital. But the launch took place in the station's VIP lounge, instead of on the platform where the huge Eurostar trains stood idle.
